title: The Decapitation — Eddie Would Go
units: Culture · 9 min read
The Decapitation
An essay on power, the fall of leaders and the void institutions are left with when they lose their visible head.
10 March 2026 · Culture
How Xi Jinping dismantled China's military command and what it means for Taiwan
«The faults of the superior man are like an eclipse: all men see them; when he corrects them, all men admire him»
— Confucius, Analects, XIX.19

At the end of January 2026, China's Ministry of Defence released a thirty-second video whose brevity belied its seismic effect. General Zhang Youxia, vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission and the second most powerful military figure in China after Xi Jinping himself, was under investigation for "serious violations of discipline and the law". The same was true of General Liu Zhenli, chief of staff of the People's Liberation Army. Within hours, their biographies vanished from official PLA websites. The two generals nominally remained on the commission, but their purge was a fact.

For those who have followed Xi Jinping's systematic consolidation of power over the last fourteen years, the announcement was surprising not for its substance (corruption investigations have become routine in China) but for its target. Zhang Youxia was no ordinary general. He was a red princeling, son of a revolutionary commander who had fought alongside Xi's father during the Chinese civil war. He was a combat veteran, one of the few senior PLA officers who had actually seen battle, having fought in the bloody border clashes with Vietnam in the late 1970s and 1980s. Most importantly, he was considered Xi's man, a confidant whose ties to the Chinese leader went back decades, whose loyalty was presumed absolute.

It was Xi himself who allowed Zhang to remain in post despite his age. When the most recent purges took place in August, the fact that the other members of the CMC (Central Military Commission) were purged and not Zhang or Liu had fostered the idea that these two generals enjoyed Xi's protection. That proved incorrect. If Zhang is not safe, then truly nobody is. And that, perhaps, was precisely the point and the message these actions were meant to convey.

Let us pause a moment on a detail of enormous importance: the PLA is not China's national army in the way the Argentine army represents the Argentine state or the United States army represents that country. The PLA is the armed wing of the Chinese Communist Party, and it answers accordingly to the organs of the party, not of the state. This has been so since its conception in the 1920s. The CMC is a party body and its members must be ratified and appointed at Communist Party plenums. And the CMC is the body that controls the PLA.
The Xi Method

To understand the significance of Zhang's fall, one must first grasp the scale of Xi Jinping's military purge. Since taking power in 2012, Xi has carried out a series of systematic purges in the party, the state and the armed forces alike. Xi has purged the PLA's top ranks with a thoroughness unprecedented in the history of the People's Republic since the purges of Mao.

Of the six generals Xi appointed to the Central Military Commission in 2022, only one remains: General Zhang Shengmin, the army's anti-corruption tsar, whose career has been as a political commissar rather than a field commander. Since 2023 alone, more than twenty senior military officers have been placed under investigation or removed. The latest investigation leaves the commission — China's supreme military decision-making body — with only two active members: Xi himself and the man running the purge.

The conventional interpretation of these purges, popular among some Western analysts, is that they reveal Xi's weakness: that he feels threatened by his generals, that the army is fractious and unreliable, that the purges are evidence of rival factions battling behind the scenes. In reality, though, the purges are not a sign of Xi's insecurity but of his absolute dominance. If the PLA does not take decisions in the manner and on the timetable the president has determined, and if its leaders show an independence that contradicts the party's ideas and strategies (that is, Xi's), nobody is exempt from removal. Not even if you shared your life with Xi, or if you are one of the last war veterans within the army.

Xi's strategy is a decapitation strategy designed to keep the PLA in check through fear. Generals are disposable. Xi can create them and he can destroy them. His capacity to do so — to remove even his closest allies, even red princelings with revolutionary pedigree — only augments his authority. This is nothing new: Mao, Stalin, the Kims, the Castro regime, all have resorted to this strategy.
The Pretext of Corruption

The official charges against Zhang and Liu were predictable: "serious violations of discipline and the law", the standard euphemism for corruption. An editorial in the PLA Daily elaborated, accusing the two generals of "gravely trampling and undermining" the Chairman Responsibility System (that is, Xi's personal authority) and of "seriously fostering political and corruption problems that weakened the Party's absolute leadership over the army".

According to a Wall Street Journal report, Zhang was accused of receiving enormous bribes in exchange for facilitating promotions within the army. The Journal reported that Zhang had allegedly leaked information to the United States about China's nuclear weapons programme — an accusation so grave that, were it true, it would constitute treason. Whether any of these charges has merit is, in the Chinese system, almost irrelevant. Most China specialists hold that while corruption concerns are real, they are typically more a pretext to justify a purge.

The deeper truth is that corruption has long been endemic in the PLA, fed by what the analyst Evan Sankey calls "a tsunami of money" poured into China's military expansion over the past two decades. When Xi first returned to Beijing in 2012, he was, according to multiple accounts, dismayed by the degree of corruption he found. The PLA had become less a revolutionary army than a bureaucracy with interests of its own, more focused on building its navy and acquiring flashy hardware than on ideological indoctrination.

Xi's solution has been methodical, but clearly directed. He introduced the Chairman Responsibility System to formalise his control over the army. In 2016 he became commander-in-chief of the PLA, claiming direct operational command rather than merely administrative control. At the 19th Party Congress in 2017, he cut the Central Military Commission from eleven members to seven, concentrating his authority. At the party plenum last October, he named the PLA's chief disciplinarian (General Zhang Shengmin) as vice-chairman of the CMC, effectively placing a political commissar with little experience above the field commanders.
The Taiwan Question

The purges inevitably raise questions about Xi's intentions towards Taiwan. Some analysts have suggested that shattering the military leadership makes an invasion of Taiwan less likely in the short term: that Xi is too busy putting the home front in order to contemplate major military action, that the disruption of command structures makes complex operations risky. Others fear the opposite is true: that by removing experienced combat veterans such as Zhang, Xi is eliminating the very voices that might counsel caution, given that these two generals were the last members of the Chinese military leadership with actual combat experience.

Other analysts, however, do not believe Xi is contemplating major military action against Taiwan in the immediate short term. Instead, Xi is looking at an American administration under Donald Trump that "does not appear particularly interested" in Taiwan, at the potential for a change of leadership in Taiwan at the 2028 elections, and calculating that now is a "safe moment to put the house in order". The purge is about long-term positioning, not imminent war.

There is also the question of Xi's own timeline. He turns seventy-three in June 2026. In October 2027, the 21st Party Congress will convene, where Xi is expected to seek a fourth five-year term. But as the specialist substack China Talk notes, the "seven up, eight down" rule — the informal age limit for Politburo membership — means that many of Xi's closest allies on the Standing Committee will be retiring. The composition of his inner circle will change dramatically. In this context the purges acquire a different meaning: they are not about preparing for war in 2026 or 2027 but about ensuring that the generals who rise to replace Zhang and the others are loyal beyond all doubt.

It is impossible to ignore, however, that there is a significant operational cost to Xi's approach. The Central Military Commission now consists essentially of Xi and a single political commissar with no command experience. The chain of command is, to put it mildly, unclear.

The purges have exposed deeper problems within the PLA. Earlier corruption scandals centred on the Rocket Force and equipment procurement, highlighting problems with readiness and capability and revealing the Chinese military as what some analysts call a potential "paper tiger" without the capacity to project power effectively. The removal of Zhang and Liu continues this pattern. Liu, as head of the Joint Staff Department, coordinated the PLA's principal combat command institution. His departure amid ongoing reforms raises obvious questions about operational continuity.

This goes to the heart of the dilemma Xi has created. By prioritising political loyalty over military competence, he may be building a more obedient PLA but not necessarily a more effective one. The lesson of Zhang's purge is clear: political loyalty comes far ahead of combat readiness. But what happens when loyalty and readiness come into tension? What happens when a politically reliable general, anxious to please Xi, assesses the PLA as ready for operations it cannot successfully execute?

The risk of miscalculation rises. Not because Xi is more likely to invade Taiwan tomorrow, but because the feedback mechanisms that might prevent disastrous errors have been systematically dismantled. The case of Russia's invasion of Ukraine comes automatically to mind.
The Historical Parallel

China, of course, has been here before. The country has a long tradition of purging senior officials, whether to root out corruption, simplify structures of government or consolidate power at the top. The most famous precedent is the Cultural Revolution, when Mao systematically destroyed much of the Party elite, including many who had been his closest comrades. A particularly relevant case is Lin Biao, Mao's designated successor and defence minister, who died mysteriously in a plane crash in 1971 while allegedly fleeing to the Soviet Union after a failed coup attempt. The circumstances of Lin's death remain murky to this day, but the lesson was clear: proximity to Mao offered no protection.

Xi's purges differ in important ways. They are more systematic, more institutionalised through anti-corruption mechanisms, visibly less chaotic than the Cultural Revolution. But the underlying logic is similar: the elimination of potential centres of power, the demonstration that nobody is indispensable, the cultivation of a generalised fear that keeps everyone in line. As with Mao, the purges serve both practical and symbolic functions. Practically, they remove potential rivals and cement Xi's control. Symbolically, they reinforce the narrative that Xi is waging a righteous battle against corruption, that only he can clean up the system.

But there is a cost. The Cultural Revolution devastated Chinese institutions and set the country's development back by years. Xi's purges may not be as destructive in scope, but they are creating institutional damage of their own. An army where generals are selected primarily for loyalty rather than competence, where speaking truth to power is potentially fatal to one's career, where the chain of command is unclear and operational continuity is constantly disrupted: such an army may look impressive on paper but could prove brittle in practice.

For the outside world, particularly for Taiwan and the United States, the purges send mixed signals. On the one hand, a PLA in turmoil is arguably less capable of mounting complex military operations in the short term. On the other, a PLA commanded by sycophants who dare not question Xi's judgement may be more dangerous in the long run. The removal of experienced combat veterans such as Zhang Youxia means there are fewer voices able to explain to Xi what war actually costs, fewer people able to assess American and Taiwanese capabilities objectively.

As for Zhang Youxia himself, his fate follows a familiar pattern in Chinese politics. Once a senior figure loses standing (for whatever reason), his fall results in accusations of a litany of crimes. Whether Zhang really leaked nuclear secrets to the United States, whether he really took massive bribes, whether he formed "political cliques" as alleged: these questions will never be answered transparently. What matters is that Xi decided Zhang had to go, and in Xi's China that decision alone is enough.

The thirty-second video was simply the announcement of a verdict already delivered. Zhang's biography disappeared from the PLA website not because he was under investigation but because, in the eyes of the system, he had already ceased to exist. We shall see the ultimate impact of these purges, and as Confucius wrote more than two thousand years ago: "The superior man does not promote a man because of his words, nor does he discard words because of the man who says them". In Xi's China, however, both the words and the man who says them can disappear with equal ease.
